summary.text: An algebraic number is a number that is a root of a nonzero polynomial in one variable with integer coefficients, or equivalently rational coefficients.
They include all integers, rational numbers and n-th roots of integers, and they are closed under addition, subtraction, multiplication and division, so they form a field.
Numbers that are not algebraic are called transcendental and include pi and e; almost all real and complex numbers are transcendental.

facts.label: Transcendental
facts.value: Pi and e are not algebraic

facts.label: Algebraic closure
facts.value: The smallest algebraically closed field containing the rationals

items.prompt: Take any fraction with an integer on top and a nonzero whole number on the bottom. Why must it count as algebraic?

options.label: It is a root of a simple nonzero polynomial with integer coefficients
It is always larger than every integer
It can always be written as a square root
It is always a root of a polynomial with pi in it

items.explain: A fraction a/b is a root of the nonzero polynomial bx − a, so it meets the definition of an algebraic number.

items.prompt: A number is not a root of any nonzero polynomial with integer coefficients. What is it called?
items.explain: Numbers that are not algebraic are called transcendental; pi and e are examples.

items.prompt: You add two algebraic numbers, then multiply the result by a third algebraic number. What can you say about the final number?
items.explain: Algebraic numbers are closed under addition, subtraction, multiplication and division, so they form a field.

items.prompt: The algebraic numbers can be counted in a list. What does that say about the transcendental numbers among the reals?

options.label: Almost all real numbers are transcendental

items.explain: Since the algebraic numbers are countable, almost all real and complex numbers are transcendental.

items.prompt: An algebraic number has a minimal polynomial of degree 1. What kind of number is it, going by the standard examples?
items.explain: All rational numbers have degree 1, while an algebraic number of degree 2 is a quadratic irrational.

items.prompt: You build a polynomial whose coefficients are themselves algebraic numbers and solve it. What can you say about its roots?
items.explain: Every root of a polynomial with algebraic coefficients is again algebraic, which means the field of algebraic numbers is algebraically closed.

paragraphs.heading: Roots of integer polynomials
paragraphs.text: An algebraic number is any number that solves a polynomial equation in one variable whose coefficients are integers, as long as the polynomial is not zero. Using rational coefficients instead gives exactly the same numbers: multiply a polynomial with fractional coefficients by their least common denominator and you get one with integer coefficients and the same roots. The golden ratio (1 + √5)/2 is an example, because it is a solution of x² − x − 1 = 0.

paragraphs.heading: Many familiar numbers qualify
paragraphs.text: Every integer and every rational number is algebraic, and so is every n-th root of an integer. A rational number a/b is the root of bx − a. The numbers √2 and ³√3/2 are roots of x² − 2 and 8x³ − 3. Complex numbers count too: 1 + i is a root of x⁴ + 4. Gaussian integers, complex numbers a + bi where a and b are both integers, are roots of x² − 2ax + a² + b².

paragraphs.heading: Degree and minimal polynomial
paragraphs.text: For each algebraic number there is exactly one monic polynomial with rational coefficients and the lowest possible degree that has it as a root; this is its minimal polynomial. For a quadratic ax² + bx + c, being monic means a = 1. If the minimal polynomial has degree n, the number is said to have degree n too. So every rational number has degree 1, while the algebraic numbers of degree 2 are the quadratic irrationals. The cosines of π/7, 3π/7 and 5π/7 all satisfy 8x³ − 4x² − 4x + 1 = 0, which is irreducible over the rationals, so they are conjugate algebraic numbers.

paragraphs.heading: A closed world
paragraphs.text: Add, subtract, multiply or divide two algebraic numbers and the answer is again algebraic, so together they form a field, written ℚ̄. The real algebraic numbers on their own form a field as well. Any expression built from algebraic numbers with finitely many arithmetic steps and n-th roots is algebraic. Even a root of a polynomial whose coefficients are algebraic numbers is algebraic, which is what it means to call this field algebraically closed. No smaller algebraically closed field contains the rationals, which is why it is named the algebraic closure of the rationals.

paragraphs.heading: Beyond roots and radicals
paragraphs.text: Some algebraic numbers cannot be written using arithmetic and n-th roots. The roots of x⁵ − x + 1 are an example: they solve a polynomial with integer coefficients, so they are algebraic, yet no such expression gives them. This happens with many, though not all, polynomials of degree 5 or more.

paragraphs.heading: Rare and everywhere at once
paragraphs.text: Numbers that are not algebraic are called transcendental, and π and e are among them. The algebraic numbers are countable, so as a part of the complex numbers their Lebesgue measure is 0: in effect they take up no room at all. That means almost all real and complex numbers are transcendental. Yet algebraic numbers are dense in the reals, because they include the rational numbers, which are themselves dense in the reals.
